justification:
No verified factual error, so not capped at 7. The article's central, load-bearing claim — 'RSA key exchange was removed in TLS 1.3' — checks out precisely: I fetched RFC 8446's plaintext edition directly and found the article's quote 'Static RSA and Diffie-Hellman cipher suites have been removed; all public-key based key exchange mechanisms now provide forward secrecy' verbatim in section 1.2 ('Major Differences from TLS 1.2'), exactly where cited. The three RFC 8446 section-1 property definitions (authentication/confidentiality/integrity) are also verbatim and correctly placed, as are the AEAD/'those that remain' quote (section 1.2), the key_share quote (section 2, with a faithful ellipsis over the elided pre_shared_key clause), the message-flow figure's brace/bracket legend (section 2), and both RFC 5280 section 3.2 quotes about certification paths and the limited root set, which I confirmed byte-for-byte against the fetched RFC text including the correctly-elided middle clause. Every Microsoft Learn quote (AesGcm.Decrypt's 'if tag cannot be validated ... then plaintext is cleared', ECDiffieHellman.DeriveKeyFromHash's 'the hash of the shared secret', ECDsa.SignHash's IeeeP1363FixedFieldConcatenation default, SslStream.RemoteCertificate's and RemoteCertificateValidationCallback's definitions, and X509Chain's 'rules governing certificate validation are complex' remark) is verbatim on the live page today. The 'starting in .NET 8' claim for AuthenticationTagMismatchException is consistent with Microsoft Learn's own version-fallback behavior (requesting ?view=net-7.0 redirects to net-10.0 with viewFallbackFrom=net-7.0, i.e. the type has no net-7.0 page; ?view=net-8.0 serves directly with no fallback). The Let's Encrypt FAQ quote about phishing/malware sites is exact, including the section heading. Code verification: I independently retyped and ran all seven executable blocks (AEAD encrypt/tamper/reject, ECDH agreement, ECDSA sign/verify against transcript/attacker, HMAC Finished match/mismatch, the live example.com chain walk, and the self-signed loopback server) outside the harness on .NET 10.0.401/Windows 11 x64, and every one produced output identical to what the article shows, with zero compiler warnings. The live chain check returned a stable 5-link chain (leaf -> Cloudflare TLS Issuing ECC CA 3 -> SSL.com TLS Transit ECC CA R2 -> SSL.com TLS ECC Root CA 2022 -> AAA Certificate Services, self-signed) across three independent runs of my own copy and five consecutive `run-code.mjs` invocations, so the CDN's current chain shape is not a flakiness source today, and the article correctly wildcards the digits and dates the specific capture rather than asserting it as permanent. The self-signed-server exercise reliably reproduced RemoteCertificateChainErrors across three of my own runs.

What holds it below 8.5, in order of weight: (1) A repeated citation-location error. Three quotes the article attributes to RFC 8446's detail subsections — 'the certificate of the endpoint and any per-certificate extensions' cited to section 4.4.2, 'a signature over the entire handshake using the private key corresponding to the public key in the Certificate message' cited to section 4.4.3, and 'provides key confirmation, binds the endpoint's identity to the exchanged keys, and in PSK mode also authenticates the handshake' cited (as 'same section' = 4.4.4) — are all real, verbatim RFC 8446 text, but I searched the full RFC and each phrase occurs exactly once, in section 2's own 'Authentication messages' summary list, not in the numbered subsections that later define those same messages in detail. A fourth quote, 'all handshake messages after the ServerHello are now encrypted,' is cited as 'same section' (section 2, from the preceding sentence) but is verbatim only in section 1.2. Every quote is accurate; every section number is wrong. This is exactly the citation-accuracy failure the editorial brief's pilot lessons name directly ('cite where the claim is made, and make sure that page supports that clause'). (2) A missing binding toolchain statement. The pilot lessons require stating the toolchain once, in the writer's own words, where measurements appear; the article has a genuine network-dependent measurement ('The run used for this page, on 2026-09-22, found five links...') but never states runtime version, OS or CPU class anywhere in the piece — unlike every other published networking article in this pillar (dns.md, http-explained.md, how-the-internet-works.md all carry an explicit '.NET 10 SDK (10.0.401) on Windows 11, x64' sentence near their first measurement). (3) Two unsourced prevalence/behavior claims with no citation: 'most servers do not use it' (TLS record padding) and the traffic-analysis fingerprinting claim that follows it — both plausible and consistent with well-known practice, but RFC 8446 itself only says padding is optional and says nothing about adoption rates or fingerprinting difficulty, and no other source in front matter supports either clause. (4) A verification-honesty note, not a rule violation but worth recording: I was asked to confirm the article discloses that it could not get a real name-mismatch certificate error against example.com because of CDN behavior, and that it dropped a nonce-reuse exercise it could not source against NIST SP 800-38D. I read the full article twice and grepped it for 'CDN', 'mismatch', 'nonce', 'NIST' and '800-38D'; no such disclosures exist anywhere in the file, in WORKLOG.md, or in docs/NEEDS_MARKUS.md. The one live-network certificate exercise in the article (the self-signed loopback server) demonstrates RemoteCertificateChainErrors (untrusted root), not a name mismatch, and the article never mentions attempting or abandoning a name-mismatch test, nor a nonce-reuse exercise of any kind. I am reporting this as a factual finding rather than confirming something I could not find: whatever produced that expectation, it does not match what is actually on disk in this worktree right now.

issues.location: "What doesn't the padlock protect against?", Traffic analysis paragraph: 'Padding is optional and most servers do not use it, so an observer ... can often still tell which page on a site you loaded'
issues.problem: RFC 8446 (the only source cited in this sentence) says padding is optional and available; it says nothing about how many servers actually enable it or how reliably page identity leaks through record sizes. No source in front matter supports either the adoption-rate claim or the fingerprinting-difficulty claim; both are stated as plain fact.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either cite a primary source for TLS padding adoption / traffic-analysis fingerprinting (e.g. a peer-reviewed website-fingerprinting paper, which the brief accepts as a primary source), or soften to something the RFC alone supports: 'padding is optional, and where it isn't used, an observer who cannot read a byte of your traffic can sometimes still infer which page you loaded from record sizes alone.'

issues.location: "See the policy error instead of just a thrown exception" exercise
issues.problem: The article's only live-network certificate-error exercise demonstrates an untrusted root (RemoteCertificateChainErrors) via a local self-signed server; it never attempts, mentions, or explains the absence of a name-mismatch (RemoteCertificateNameMismatch) demonstration, even though a mismatched hostname is arguably the padlock failure a reader is more likely to have actually seen in a browser. This is a coverage gap, not an error, and does not by itself require a live example.com call (a second local server presenting a cert for the wrong name would demonstrate it without any network dependency at all).
issues.fixLooksLike: Either add a short second exercise/paragraph covering RemoteCertificateNameMismatch with a second self-signed server whose SAN doesn't match TargetHost, or add one sentence acknowledging the exercise covers only the chain-trust failure mode and not the name-mismatch one.
